action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

edits.description: publish: small changes Claude makes to the file at `file_path` in this same call, instead of editing the file with Edit and publishing after. Use it on a page (add `url` to update an artifact from another conversation) or on one data file of an artifact made from a type (its `url`, with that file as `file_path`). Not allowed with `type_url` or `files`. Each old_str is text copied exactly from the file as it now stands and must occur in it exactly once; new_str takes its place (empty deletes it). The edits apply in order, all or none: the file is published with them and then saved with them on disk, so it stays the source for later changes; on a miss nothing is changed or published, and the result says which edit failed and why.

old_str.description: Text copied exactly from the file; must occur once.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes the published path of a `files` entry. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` is served at its path relative to `root`, unless a `files` map entry states its served path. Claude sends it with every such publish, set to the folder that holds the Artifact's files at their served paths.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

page_token.description: list only: the `next_page_token` a listing of the same scope gave, to list the artifacts after it.

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (writing people will keep editing or pass around as text, such as a memo, plan, spec, proposal or notes), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (a page to look at or use: an explainer, a diagram, anything interactive, a dashboard that shows data, anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

| `taxonomy.json` | Original code, name, parent grouping, policy grouping and theme; no policy prose or company decisions |
| `taxonomy-provenance.json` | Read-only SQL, origin, row count, extraction time and taxonomy digest |
| `resources.json` | Curated resource IDs, URLs, evidence URLs, roles, topic selections, rationale, access notes and caveats |
| `resource-review.json` | Review date and resource-file digest, source-access limitations and standards references |
| `queries/*.rq` | Runnable SPARQL queries for categories, proposed links and conflicting scores |

**Namespace:** `https://ethicic.com/ns/exclusions/` is a **proposed** namespace
under Ethical Capital's existing domain. These IRIs are used consistently in
the files; no dereferenceable routes have been deployed. Select and review the
public persistence policy before publication. No `owl:imports`, `owl:sameAs`,
`owl:equivalentClass`, `skos:exactMatch` or `skos:closeMatch` is emitted.

The graph reuses [SKOS](https://www.w3.org/TR/skos-reference/) for concepts,
[DCAT 3](https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-dcat-3/) for the catalog,
[PROV-O](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/) for attribution, and
[JSON-LD 1.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/json-ld11/) for JSON serialization. Standard
namespace spellings are preserved, including their original HTTP IRIs.

`ec:Assessment` requires an assessed entity, versioned criterion and policy,
outcome, evidence, publisher attribution and review state. `ec:Criterion`
and `ec:Policy` require explicit versions. Evidence needs its source and
attribution. Outcomes include excluded, observation, not excluded under this
policy, unknown and revoked. A missing decision is unknown, not approval;
“not excluded” is also scoped to one policy, not an ethical certification.
Known validity dates may be recorded separately from capture/publication time.

`ec:LinkAssertion` describes a **proposed** `rdfs:seeAlso` link. It does not
assert the proposed triple itself. The catalog's actual `dcat:landingPage`
links make the external resources discoverable. Links record local draft
curation by a software agent, not endorsement or agreement by any publisher.

Original parent/policy grouping labels are retained as literals. No inferred
`skos:broader` hierarchy repairs the source: for example, the database groups
“Environmental Damage” under product-based exclusions. These inconsistencies
remain visible rather than becoming stronger logical assertions.

## 5. The loop

Build -> profile checks -> mutation tests -> independent RDF parse and graph
comparison -> SPARQL queries. Rebuilding with identical inputs must reproduce
identical output. The graph binds the existing corpus snapshot by digest;
refreshing that corpus requires rebuilding the linked data.

Assumptions and limits: category names do not specify thresholds; topic links
are draft curation; domain matches join registry records to resource websites,
not companies to legal entities. Similar names, tickers, parent companies,
brands and ownership relationships never establish entity identity. An
exclusion does not automatically propagate across ownership links.

## 6. Supply chain and isolation

Runtime: Python 3 standard library, governed by the Python Software Foundation.
Independent verifier: RDFLib 7.1.4 (development only), with resolver-selected
transitive dependencies. No new runtime service or global tool is installed.
`export_taxonomy.py` additionally uses the existing database environment's
`psycopg2`, in a read-only transaction. Default build never invokes that export.

Publicly accessible does not mean openly reusable. OpenSanctions and Invest
Your Values document commercial licensing requirements. The catalog stores
links and our descriptions, not copies of those datasets. Underlying source
licenses do not license this repository or resolve G2, G5 or G9.

# Exclusion categories → SDG targets and indicators

A crosswalk from Ethical Capital's 59 exclusion categories (the harms
topology in `linked-data/taxonomy.json`) to the UN Sustainable Development
Goals, at target and indicator level.

It has two layers, and they are kept apart on purpose:

| Layer | File | Who decides | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Computed | `computed.tsv` | A literal string match, re-run by `crosswalk.py` | Deterministic, but it rests on `lexicon.tsv`, which is a proposal |
| Proposed | `proposed.tsv` | A language model's judgment | Proposal; every row `review_status=proposed` |

`gaps.tsv` is built from both layers. It lists what neither layer reaches.

## Files

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `MANIFEST.tsv` | Each source: URL, local path, bytes, SHA-256, BLAKE3, fetch date (2026-11-04), role |
| `crosswalk.py` | Stdlib PEP 723 script: `fetch`, `build`, `verify` |
| `lexicon.tsv` | Category code → literal terms. Authored judgment. **STATUS: proposal (witness llm:claude-opus-5-5 prompt=unrecorded)** until Sloane approves it |
| `computed.tsv` | One row per (category, SDG code, lexicon term, sentence) match: `category, sdg_code, sdg_level, sdg_uri, match_term, lexicon_row, span_start, span_end, span_text, span_sha256` |
| `proposed.tsv` | Model-proposed links: `category, sdg_target, relation, target_quote, rationale, witness, review_status` |
| `gaps.tsv` | Categories with no computed match, categories with nothing at all, goals reached only by proposals, lexicon terms that occur nowhere in the SDG text, and targets nothing reaches |
| `sdg-index.tsv` | Every goal, target and indicator in the pinned framework: code, UNSD indicator code, UN Library URI, text length and SHA-256. Codes and hashes only, no text |

Category IRIs follow `linked-data`: `https://ethicic.com/ns/exclusions/category/<code>`.
SDG URIs come from the UN Library's SKOS vocabulary: goals and targets are
`http://metadata.un.org/sdg/<code>` (for example `.../sdg/8.7`), and
indicators are `http://metadata.un.org/sdg/<UNSD code>` (for example
`.../sdg/C080701`). A URI is written only if it exists in the pinned SKOS
dump.

## Sources

1. **UNSD global indicator framework, after the 2026 refinement** (English
   xlsx), linked from <https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/indicators/indicators-list/>.
   This is the official text of the 17 goals, the 169 targets and the
   indicators, with UNSD indicator codes. The parse finds 17 goals, 169
   targets and 251 indicator listings with 235 distinct UNSD codes. The
   landing page says the framework "includes 234 unique indicators" out of 251
   listed, because thirteen repeat. The one-code difference is unresolved;
   the page notes that 13.2.1/13.b.1 repeat "(with a slight amendment)",
   which may explain it. Not checked.
2. **The landing page itself**, pinned for its version statement (it lists the
   refinements through the 57th Statistical Commission, March 2026,
   E/CN.3/2026/12). These saved bytes are the pin; the live page will not
   re-fetch byte-identically.
3. **UN Library SDG Taxonomy (SKOS)**, `sdg-20230317.ttl`, linked from
   <https://research.un.org/en/thesaurus/downloads>. It is used only for URIs.
   It is the March 2023 dump, so it is older than the 2026 framework: 10
   indicator codes have no URI in it (2.2.4, 3.8.2, 3.b.3, 4.6.1, 8.9.2,
   11.c.1, 12.7.1, 13.2.1, 13.b.1, 15.9.1), and their `sdg_uri` is blank.
   The live service at <https://metadata.un.org/sdg/> answers content
   negotiation (`Accept: text/turtle`) per concept, but it offers no newer
   full download.
4. **`linked-data/taxonomy.json`**, the local read-only input that defines the
   59 categories. It was uncommitted work in another session when it was
   pinned; its hash is in `MANIFEST.tsv`, so a change to it fails `verify`.

### Terms of use (verbatim)

UNSD pages link to the United Nations website terms,
<https://www.un.org/en/about-us/terms-of-use> (retrieved 2026-11-04):

> (a) The United Nations maintains this web site (the “Site”) as a courtesy to those who may choose to access the Site (“Users”). The information presented herein is for informative purposes only. The United Nations grants permission to Users to visit the Site and to download and copy the information, documents and materials (collectively, “Materials”) from the Site for the User’s personal, non-commercial use, without any right to resell or redistribute them or to compile or create derivative works therefrom, subject to the terms and conditions outlined below, and also subject to more specific restrictions that may apply to specific Material within this Site.

<https://www.un.org/en/about-us/copyright> (retrieved 2026-11-04):

> None of the materials provided on this web site may be used, reproduced or transmitted, in whole or in part, in any form or by any means, electronic or mechanical, including photocopying, recording or the use of any information storage and retrieval system, except as provided for in the Terms and Conditions of Use of United Nations Web Sites, without permission in writing from the publisher.

The UN Library SDG Taxonomy, <https://research.un.org/en/thesaurus/downloads>
(retrieved 2026-11-04):

> The SDG Knowledge Organization System, accessible at http://metadata.un.org/sdg , is made available free of charge and may be copied freely, duplicated and further distributed with the following citation: © United Nations, 2023, http://metadata.un.org/sdg/ Information downloaded on [DATE]

Citation for the URIs used here: © United Nations, 2023,
http://metadata.un.org/sdg/ Information downloaded on 2026-11-04.

**What this means for the repository.** The framework text falls under the
un.org terms: personal, non-commercial use, with no redistribution and no
derivative works. So the framework file stays in the gitignored `.cache/`.
The repository commits only codes, hashes, offsets, and quotations of
individual targets and indicators: `span_text` in `computed.tsv` and
`target_quote` in `proposed.tsv`. Whether those quotations are short enough
is a judgment for a person to make. `computed.tsv` quotes whole sentences. It
covers 92 of the 420 target and indicator codes, which is about 16,000 of the
roughly 61,000 characters of target and indicator text. If that is too much,
change the span to a window around the match. The hashes and offsets would
still let `verify` check it.

## Rebuild

From this directory:

    uv run crosswalk.py fetch    # download the sources into .cache/ and check hashes
    uv run crosswalk.py build    # write sdg-index.tsv, computed.tsv, gaps.tsv
    uv run crosswalk.py verify   # rebuild in memory, compare bytes, re-slice spans, check quotes

`build` stops if any source's bytes or SHA-256 differ from `MANIFEST.tsv`.
`verify` checks four things. The rebuild must match the committed files byte
for byte. Every `span_text` must re-slice from the pinned text at its offsets
and match its SHA-256. Every `target_quote` must occur verbatim in its pinned
target. Every proposed category and target must exist.

The source text contains no-break spaces (U+00A0, as in "40 per cent") and
non-breaking hyphens (U+2011, as in "non‑communicable"). Quotes copy them
exactly. Matching is literal: a lexicon term with an ordinary hyphen or space
will not match those characters.

## Layer 1: computed

The lexicon, read against the official target and indicator text:

- Matching ignores case and treats each term literally, with no stemming. A
  term counts only where no letter or digit sits directly before or after it,
  so "arms" does not match "farms" or "firearms".
- Text is split into sentences at `.` or `;` followed by whitespace. One row is
  written per matching sentence.
- Rows are sorted by category, then SDG code in natural order, then lexicon
  row, then offset.

A computed row means that a word appears in the text. It does not tell you
which way the target points. For example, `fossil_fuels` → 7.a is a computed
match, but target 7.a *promotes* "advanced and cleaner fossil-fuel
technology". Matches can also be off-topic: `discrimination` → 17.10 is about
trade ("non‑discriminatory … trading system"), and `regulatory_failures` →
3.d.1 refers to the International Health Regulations. The computed layer
reports these matches and does not interpret them.

The lexicon is judgment, and it is labelled that way. Two terms were dropped
while it was drafted. "occupation" occurs only in the employment sense
(8.5.1), and "conflict" also matched "conflict resolution" (16.3.1), so it was
narrowed to "conflict-related" and "conflict-affected". Two categories have no
lexicon rows: `exploitative_entertainment`, because `taxonomy.json` does not
define its scope, and `multiple_violations`, because it is a meta-category.

## Layer 2: proposed

There are 166 rows covering 57 of the 59 categories and 66 distinct targets:
97 rows are `harms` and 69 are `relates`. In a `harms` row, the excluded
activity works against what the target seeks. A `relates` row means the
category bears on the target in some other way: the bearing is indirect, it is
contested, or the target pulls the other way. For example, target 3.8 counts
opioids among essential medicines, and target 7.a promotes cleaner fossil-fuel
technology. Every row carries `witness=llm:claude-opus-5-5 prompt=unrecorded`
and `review_status=proposed`. No row has been reviewed by a person.

| | Categories |
|---|---|
| At least 1 computed match | 37 |
| At least 1 proposed target | 57 |
| Both | 37 |
| Proposal only, no computed match | 20 |
| Neither (`exclus

`computed.tsv` has 147 rows: 83 on targets and 64 on indicators, across 92
distinct codes. All 17 goals are reached by at least one layer. Goal 1 is
reached only by proposals.

## Findings from the gaps

These are findings about how far the SDG text reaches. They are not defects
to fix by adding more terms.

- **The SDG text names no fossil fuel.** "coal", "oil", "petroleum" and
  "natural gas" occur in no target or indicator. "fossil-fuel" occurs in only
  two places: 12.c, which asks states to rationalize fossil-fuel subsidies,
  and 7.a, which *promotes* cleaner fossil-fuel technology. None of the seven
  fossil-fuel value-chain categories has a computed match except
  `fossil_fuels`.
- **Animals appear only as resources.** Animals come up as genetic resources
  (2.5), as fish stocks (14.4), and as protected species when poaching or
  trafficking is illegal (15.7, 15.c). "meat", "dairy", "eggs", "leather",
  "fur", "factory farming", "animal testing" and "zoo" occur nowhere. No
  target addresses animal welfare, farmed fur, or lawful captivity.
- **The SDGs say nothing about the legal arms trade.** "arms" occurs only in
  "illicit financial and arms flows" (16.4, 16.4.2). "weapons", "firearms" and
  "military" occur nowhere.
- **Corporate political conduct is absent.** "lobbying", "political
  contributions", "competition", "monopoly", "rent-seeking" and "predatory"
  occur nowhere. Where the targets address institutions (16.6, 16.7), they
  address states.
- **The digital harms are missing.** "privacy", "personal data",
  "surveillance", "misinformation" and "disinformation" occur nowhere. The
  closest target is 16.10 ("protect fundamental freedoms").
- **Several addictive products go unnamed.** Tobacco and alcohol are named
  (3.a, 3.5). "opioid" and "gambling" are not. Opioids fall under
  "narcotic drug abuse" (3.5) and also among essential medicines (3.8).
- **Some identity and rights grounds are missing.** The grounds listed in
  10.2 ("age, sex, disability, race, ethnicity, origin, religion or economic
  or other status") do not name sexual orientation or gender identity. The
  Indigenous targets concern land access and benefit-sharing (2.3, 15.6),
  not free, prior and informed consent. No target mentions occupation of
  territory.
- **103 of the 169 targets are reached by neither layer.** Most are means of
  implementation (the 17.x targets and the lettered targets) and
  service-delivery targets, which exclusion categories do not address.

The full list is `gaps.tsv`. It is rebuilt from the data and never edited by
hand.

## What this does not answer

- **It does not say that any company harms any target.** A category is a
  class of activity or conduct. Excluding a company is a separate assessment
  with its own evidence, and that assessment lives elsewhere.
- **It does not validate the SDGs as complete.** It does not use them as a
  measure of harm either. The gaps above show that the framework is silent on
  much of what the exclusion policy covers. A category with no SDG link is not
  less serious for that.
- **It does not establish the direction of a computed match.** Only a reviewed
  proposal can do that.
- **It does not interpret the category definitions.** It works from category
  names and groupings in `taxonomy.json`, which carry no thresholds or policy
  prose.
- **It does not cover the 2030 Agenda declaration or preamble**, only the
  goals, targets and indicators. The declaration's paragraphs, for example on
  foreign occupation, are not in the pinned framework file.

# Exclusion categories → SDG targets and indicators

A crosswalk from Ethical Capital's 59 exclusion categories (the harms
topology in `linked-data/taxonomy.json`) to the UN Sustainable Development
Goals, at target and indicator level.

It has two layers, and they are kept apart on purpose:

| Layer | File | Who decides | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Computed | `computed.tsv` | A literal string match, re-run by `crosswalk.py` | Deterministic, but it rests on `lexicon.tsv`, which is a proposal |
| Proposed | `proposed.tsv` | A language model's judgment | Proposal; every row `review_status=proposed` |

`gaps.tsv` is built from both layers. It lists what neither layer reaches.

## Files

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `MANIFEST.tsv` | Each source: URL, local path, bytes, SHA-256, BLAKE3, fetch date (2026-11-04), role |
| `crosswalk.py` | Stdlib PEP 723 script: `fetch`, `build`, `verify` |
| `lexicon.tsv` | Category code → literal terms. Authored judgment. **STATUS: proposal (witness llm:claude-opus-5-5 prompt=unrecorded)** until Sloane approves it |
| `computed.tsv` | One row per (category, SDG code, lexicon term, sentence) match: `category, sdg_code, sdg_level, sdg_uri, match_term, lexicon_row, span_start, span_end, span_text, span_sha256` |
| `proposed.tsv` | Model-proposed links: `category, sdg_target, relation, target_quote, rationale, witness, review_status` |
| `gaps.tsv` | Categories with no computed match, categories with nothing at all, goals reached only by proposals, lexicon terms that occur nowhere in the SDG text, and targets nothing reaches |
| `sdg-index.tsv` | Every goal, target and indicator in the pinned framework: code, UNSD indicator code, UN Library URI, text length and SHA-256. Codes and hashes only, no text |

Category IRIs follow `linked-data`: `https://ethicic.com/ns/exclusions/category/<code>`.
SDG URIs come from the UN Library's SKOS vocabulary: goals and targets are
`http://metadata.un.org/sdg/<code>` (for example `.../sdg/8.7`), and
indicators are `http://metadata.un.org/sdg/<UNSD code>` (for example
`.../sdg/C080701`). A URI is written only if it exists in the pinned SKOS
dump.

## Sources

1. **UNSD global indicator framework, after the 2026 refinement** (English
   xlsx), linked from <https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/indicators/indicators-list/>.
   This is the official text of the 17 goals, the 169 targets and the
   indicators, with UNSD indicator codes. The parse finds 17 goals, 169
   targets and 251 indicator listings with 235 distinct UNSD codes. The
   landing page says the framework "includes 234 unique indicators" out of 251
   listed, because thirteen repeat. The one-code difference is unresolved;
   the page notes that 13.2.1/13.b.1 repeat "(with a slight amendment)",
   which may explain it. Not checked.
2. **The landing page itself**, pinned for its version statement (it lists the
   refinements through the 57th Statistical Commission, March 2026,
   E/CN.3/2026/12). These saved bytes are the pin; the live page will not
   re-fetch byte-identically.
3. **UN Library SDG Taxonomy (SKOS)**, `sdg-20230317.ttl`, linked from
   <https://research.un.org/en/thesaurus/downloads>. It is used only for URIs.
   It is the March 2023 dump, so it is older than the 2026 framework: 10
   indicator codes have no URI in it (2.2.4, 3.8.2, 3.b.3, 4.6.1, 8.9.2,
   11.c.1, 12.7.1, 13.2.1, 13.b.1, 15.9.1), and their `sdg_uri` is blank.
   The live service at <https://metadata.un.org/sdg/> answers content
   negotiation (`Accept: text/turtle`) per concept, but it offers no newer
   full download.
4. **`linked-data/taxonomy.json`**, the local read-only input that defines the
   59 categories. It was uncommitted work in another session when it was
   pinned; its hash is in `MANIFEST.tsv`, so a change to it fails `verify`.

### Terms of use (verbatim)

UNSD pages link to the United Nations website terms,
<https://www.un.org/en/about-us/terms-of-use> (retrieved 2026-11-04):

> (a) The United Nations maintains this web site (the “Site”) as a courtesy to those who may choose to access the Site (“Users”). The information presented herein is for informative purposes only. The United Nations grants permission to Users to visit the Site and to download and copy the information, documents and materials (collectively, “Materials”) from the Site for the User’s personal, non-commercial use, without any right to resell or redistribute them or to compile or create derivative works therefrom, subject to the terms and conditions outlined below, and also subject to more specific restrictions that may apply to specific Material within this Site.

<https://www.un.org/en/about-us/copyright> (retrieved 2026-11-04):

> None of the materials provided on this web site may be used, reproduced or transmitted, in whole or in part, in any form or by any means, electronic or mechanical, including photocopying, recording or the use of any information storage and retrieval system, except as provided for in the Terms and Conditions of Use of United Nations Web Sites, without permission in writing from the publisher.

The UN Library SDG Taxonomy, <https://research.un.org/en/thesaurus/downloads>
(retrieved 2026-11-04):

> The SDG Knowledge Organization System, accessible at http://metadata.un.org/sdg , is made available free of charge and may be copied freely, duplicated and further distributed with the following citation: © United Nations, 2023, http://metadata.un.org/sdg/ Information downloaded on [DATE]

Citation for the URIs used here: © United Nations, 2023,
http://metadata.un.org/sdg/ Information downloaded on 2026-11-04.

**What this means for the repository.** The framework text falls under the
un.org terms: personal, non-commercial use, with no redistribution and no
derivative works. So the framework file stays in the gitignored `.cache/`.
The repository commits only codes, hashes, offsets, and quotations of
individual targets and indicators: `span_text` in `computed.tsv` and
`target_quote` in `proposed.tsv`. Whether those quotations are short enough
is a judgment for a person to make. `computed.tsv` quotes whole sentences. It
covers 92 of the 420 target and indicator codes, which is about 16,000 of the
roughly 61,000 characters of target and indicator text. If that is too much,
change the span to a window around the match. The hashes and offsets would
still let `verify` check it.

## Rebuild

From this directory:

    uv run crosswalk.py fetch    # download the sources into .cache/ and check hashes
    uv run crosswalk.py build    # write sdg-index.tsv, computed.tsv, gaps.tsv
    uv run crosswalk.py verify   # rebuild in memory, compare bytes, re-slice spans, check quotes

`build` stops if any source's bytes or SHA-256 differ from `MANIFEST.tsv`.
`verify` checks four things. The rebuild must match the committed files byte
for byte. Every `span_text` must re-slice from the pinned text at its offsets
and match its SHA-256. Every `target_quote` must occur verbatim in its pinned
target. Every proposed category and target must exist.

The source text contains no-break spaces (U+00A0, as in "40 per cent") and
non-breaking hyphens (U+2011, as in "non‑communicable"). Quotes copy them
exactly. Matching is literal: a lexicon term with an ordinary hyphen or space
will not match those characters.

## Layer 1: computed

The lexicon, read against the official target and indicator text:

- Matching ignores case and treats each term literally, with no stemming. A
  term counts only where no letter or digit sits directly before or after it,
  so "arms" does not match "farms" or "firearms".
- Text is split into sentences at `.` or `;` followed by whitespace. One row is
  written per matching sentence.
- Rows are sorted by category, then SDG code in natural order, then lexicon
  row, then offset.

A computed row means that a word appears in the text. It does not tell you
which way the target points. For example, `fossil_fuels` → 7.a is a computed
match, but target 7.a *promotes* "advanced and cleaner fossil-fuel
technology". Matches can also be off-topic: `discrimination` → 17.10 is about
trade ("non‑discriminatory … trading system"), and `regulatory_failures` →
3.d.1 refers to the International Health Regulations. The computed layer
reports these matches and does not interpret them.

The lexicon is judgment, and it is labelled that way. Two terms were dropped
while it was drafted. "occupation" occurs only in the employment sense
(8.5.1), and "conflict" also matched "conflict resolution" (16.3.1), so it was
narrowed to "conflict-related" and "conflict-affected". Two categories have no
lexicon rows: `exploitative_entertainment`, because `taxonomy.json` does not
define its scope, and `multiple_violations`, because it is a meta-category.

## Layer 2: proposed

There are 166 rows covering 57 of the 59 categories and 66 distinct targets:
97 rows are `harms` and 69 are `relates`. In a `harms` row, the excluded
activity works against what the target seeks. A `relates` row means the
category bears on the target in some other way: the bearing is indirect, it is
contested, or the target pulls the other way. For example, target 3.8 counts
opioids among essential medicines, and target 7.a promotes cleaner fossil-fuel
technology. Every row carries `witness=llm:claude-opus-5-5 prompt=unrecorded`
and `review_status=proposed`. No row has been reviewed by a person.

## Counts (out of 59 categories)

| | Categories |
|---|---|
| At least 1 computed match | 37 |
| At least 1 proposed target | 57 |
| Both | 37 |
| Proposal only, no computed match | 20 |

## Findings from the gaps

These are findings about how far the SDG text reaches. They are not defects
to fix by adding more terms.

- **Animals appear only as resources.** Animals come up as genetic resources
  (2.5), as fish stocks (14.4), and as protected species when poaching or
  trafficking is illegal (15.7, 15.c). "meat", "dairy", "eggs", "leather",
  "fur", "factory farming", "animal testing" and "zoo" occur nowhere. No
  target addresses animal welfare, farmed fur, or lawful captivity.
- **The SDGs say nothing about the legal arms trade.** "arms" occurs only in
  "illicit financial and arms flows" (16.4, 16.4.2). "weapons", "firearms" and
  "military" occur nowhere.
- **Corporate political conduct is absent.** "lobbying", "political
  contributions", "competition", "monopoly", "rent-seeking" and "predatory"
  occur nowhere. Where the targets address institutions (16.6, 16.7), they
  address states.
- **The digital harms are missing.** "privacy", "personal data",
  "surveillance", "misinformation" and "disinformation" occur nowhere. The
  closest target is 16.10 ("protect fundamental freedoms").
- **Several addictive products go unnamed.** Tobacco and alcohol are named
  (3.a, 3.5). "opioid" and "gambling" are not. Opioids fall under

  implementation (the 17.x targets and the lettered targets) and
  service-delivery targets, which exclusion categories do not address.

The full list is `gaps.tsv`. It is rebuilt from the data and never edited by
hand.

## What this does not answer

- **It does not say that any company harms any target.** A category is a
  class of activity or conduct. Excluding a company is a separate assessment
  with its own evidence, and that assessment lives elsewhere.
- **It does not validate the SDGs as complete.** It does not use them as a

81	**What this means for the repository.** The framework text falls under the
82	un.org terms: personal, non-commercial use, with no redistribution and no
83	derivative works. So the framework file stays in the gitignored `.cache/`.
84	The repository commits only codes, hashes, offsets, and quotations of
85	individual targets and indicators: `span_text` in `computed.tsv` and
86	`target_quote` in `proposed.tsv`. Whether those quotations are short enough
87	is a judgment for a person to make. `computed.tsv` quotes whole sentences. It
88	covers 92 of the 420 target and indicator codes, which is about 16,000 of the
89	roughly 61,000 characters of target and indicator text. If that is too much,
90	change the span to a window around the match. The hashes and offsets would
91	still let `verify` check it.
92	
93	## Rebuild
94	
95	From this directory:
96	
97	    uv run crosswalk.py fetch    # download the sources into .cache/ and check hashes
98	    uv run crosswalk.py build    # write sdg-index.tsv, computed.tsv, gaps.tsv
99	    uv run crosswalk.py verify   # rebuild in memory, compare bytes, re-slice spans, check quotes
100	
101	`build` stops if any source's bytes or SHA-256 differ from `MANIFEST.tsv`.
102	`verify` checks four things. The rebuild must match the committed files byte
103	for byte. Every `span_text` must re-slice from the pinned text at its offsets
104	and match its SHA-256. Every `target_quote` must occur verbatim in its pinned
105	target. Every proposed category and target must exist.
106	
107	The source text contains no-break spaces (U+00A0, as in "40 per cent") and
108	non-breaking hyphens (U+2011, as in "non‑communicable"). Quotes copy them
109	exactly. Matching is literal: a lexicon term with an ordinary hyphen or space
110	will not match those characters.
111	
112	## Layer 1: computed
113	
114	The lexicon, read against the official target and indicator text:
115	
116	- Matching ignores case and treats each term literally, with no stemming. A
117	  term counts only where no letter or digit sits directly before or after it,
118	  so "arms" does not match "farms" or "firearms".
119	- Text is split into sentences at `.` or `;` followed by whitespace. One row is
120	  written per matching sentence.
121	- Rows are sorted by category, then SDG code in natural order, then lexicon
122	  row, then offset.
123	
124	A computed row means that a word appears in the text. It does not tell you
125	which way the target points. For example, `fossil_fuels` → 7.a is a computed
126	match, but target 7.a *promotes* "advanced and cleaner fossil-fuel
127	technology". Matches can also be off-topic: `discrimination` → 17.10 is about
128	trade ("non‑discriminatory … trading system"), and `regulatory_failures` →
129	3.d.1 refers to the International Health Regulations. The computed layer
130	reports these matches and does not interpret them.
131	
132	The lexicon is judgment, and it is labelled that way. Two terms were dropped
133	while it was drafted. "occupation" occurs only in the employment sense
134	(8.5.1), and "conflict" also matched "conflict resolution" (16.3.1), so it was

un.org terms: personal, non-commercial use, with no redistribution and no
derivative works. So the framework file stays in the gitignored `.cache/`.
The repository commits only codes, hashes, offsets, and quotations of
individual targets and indicators: `span_text` in `computed.tsv` and
`target_quote` in `proposed.tsv`. Whether those quotations are short enough
is a judgment for a person to make. `computed.tsv` quotes whole sentences. It
covers 92 of the 420 target and indicator codes, which is about 16,000 of the
roughly 61,000 characters of target and indicator text. If that is too much,
change the span to a window around the match. The hashes and offsets would
still let `verify` check it.

## Rebuild

From this directory:

    uv run crosswalk.py fetch    # download the sources into .cache/ and check hashes
    uv run crosswalk.py build    # write sdg-index.tsv, computed.tsv, gaps.tsv
    uv run crosswalk.py verify   # rebuild in memory, compare bytes, re-slice spans, check quotes

`build` stops if any source's bytes or SHA-256 differ from `MANIFEST.tsv`.
`verify` checks four things. The rebuild must match the committed files byte
for byte. Every `span_text` must re-slice from the pinned text at its offsets
and match its SHA-256. Every `target_quote` must occur verbatim in its pinned
target. Every proposed category and target must exist.

The source text contains no-break spaces (U+00A0, as in "40 per cent") and
non-breaking hyphens (U+2011, as in "non‑communicable"). Quotes copy them
exactly. Matching is literal: a lexicon term with an ordinary hyphen or space
will not match those characters.

## Layer 1: computed

The lexicon, read against the official target and indicator text:

- Matching ignores case and treats each term literally, with no stemming. A
  term counts only where no letter or digit sits directly before or after it,
  so "arms" does not match "farms" or "firearms".
- Text is split into sentences at `.` or `;` followed by whitespace. One row is
  written per matching sentence.
- Rows are sorted by category, then SDG code in natural order, then lexicon
  row, then offset.

A computed row means that a word appears in the text. It does not tell you
which way the target points. For example, `fossil_fuels` → 7.a is a computed
match, but target 7.a *promotes* "advanced and cleaner fossil-fuel
technology". Matches can also be off-topic: `discrimination` → 17.10 is about
trade ("non‑discriminatory … trading system"), and `regulatory_failures` →
3.d.1 refers to the International Health Regulations. The computed layer
reports these matches and does not interpret them.

The lexicon is judgment, and it is labelled that way. Two terms were dropped
while it was drafted. "occupation" occurs only in the employment sense
(8.5.1), and "conflict" also matched "conflict resolution" (16.3.1), so it was

The sentence is kept only as offsets and SHA-256; `window_text` is at most 80 characters around the match; `direction` is always `unassessed` |"),
("""individual targets and indicators: `span_text` in `computed.tsv` and

is a judgment for a person to make. `computed.tsv` quotes whole sentences. It

"""individual targets and indicators, each at most 80 characters and cut at
word boundaries: `window_text` in `computed.tsv` and `target_quote` in

across 123 codes, which is 17.1% of the 60,809 characters of target and
indicator text. `gaps.tsv` and `sdg-index.tsv` hold codes and hashes only."""),
("""for byte. Every `span_text` must re-slice from the pinned text at its offsets
and match its SHA-256. Every `target_quote` must occur verbatim in its pinned
target. Every proposed category and target must exist.""",
"""for byte. Every sentence span must re-slice from the pinned text at its
offsets to its SHA-256, and every `window_text` must re-slice inside that
sentence, contain the term and be at most 80 characters. Every `target_quote`
must be at most 80 characters and occur verbatim in its pinned target. Every
proposed category and target must exist."""),
("""The source text contains no-break spaces (U+00A0, as in "40 per cent") and
non-breaking hyphens (U+2011, as in "non‑communicable"). Quotes copy them
exactly. Matching is literal: a lexicon term with an ordinary hyphen or space
will not match those characters.""",
"""**Known recall limit.** The source text contains no-break spaces (U+00A0,
as in "40 per cent") and non-breaking hyphens (U+2011, as in
"non‑communicable"). They are not normalised: quotes and windows copy them
exactly, and matching is literal, so a lexicon term written with an ordinary
space or hyphen misses any occurrence that uses those characters. Some real
matches may therefore be absent from `computed.tsv`."""),
("""  written per matching sentence.""",
"""  written per matching sentence, using the sentence's first match for the
  window."""),
("""A computed row means that a word appears in the text. It does not tell you
which way the target points. For example,""",
"""A computed match says a lexicon word appears in the target, not whether the
target opposes or promotes the activity; every row carries
`direction=unassessed`. For example,"""),
("""trade ("non‑discriminatory … trading system"), and""", """trade, and"""),
]
for a,b in R:
    assert s.count(a)==1, a[:60]; s=s.replace(a,b)
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
EOF

Done. Rebuilt twice with identical SHA-256 for all four TSVs, and `verify` passes under `uv run`. No git writes and no rule breaks.

- **computed.tsv** (35.6 KB, was 49.0 KB): each match now shows at most 80 characters around the word, cut at word boundaries and copied exactly from the source. The full sentence is kept only as offsets plus its SHA-256. Every row has `direction` set to `unassessed`. `verify` now checks that the sentence hash matches, that the window sits inside its sentence and contains the term, that it is at most 80 characters, and that `direction` is `unassessed`.
- **proposed.tsv**: I shortened 32 quotes to at most 80 characters, still verbatim. `verify` now enforces that limit.
- **gaps.tsv and sdg-index.tsv**: codes and hashes only.
- **README**: quotes shortened, plus the direction sentence (with 7.a). No-break spaces and hyphens are not normalised; they are listed as a known recall limit.

Quoted text now covers 10,388 distinct characters across 123 codes, which is 17.1% of the 60,809 characters of target and indicator text. Before, `computed.tsv` alone was about 27%.
